## Results

### CCC-RISE framework overview

::: {#fig-1}
![](figures/figure1/figure1.svg){width="6.5in"}

**CCC-RISE deconvolves variation in communication across single cells and conditions.** ({{< panel 1 workflow.1 >}}) RISE projects multi-condition scRNA-seq data into eigen-states and decomposes the resulting aligned condition by eigen-state by gene tensor.
({{< panel 1 workflow.2 >}}) Communication scores are computed between eigen-states for ligand--receptor (LR) pairs to form a 4D communication tensor.
({{< panel 1 workflow.3 >}}) CPD decomposes the communication tensor into factors describing variation across conditions, sender eigen-states, receiver eigen-states, and LR pairs.
({{< panel 1 embedding >}}) RISE projections serve as a common embedding basis to visualize cell-to-cell heterogeneity across all conditions.
({{< panel 1 cell-mapping >}}) Sender and receiver eigen-state factors and RISE projections collectively map communication patterns back to single cells.
({{< panel 1 component-interpretation >}}) Each CCC-RISE component represents a communication program defined by the association weights across four dimensions: experimental conditions, sender cells, receiver cells, and LR pairs.
:::

RISE projects cells from multiple conditions onto a shared set of eigen-states, effectively aligning them based on gene expression without requiring *a priori* labeling ({{< fig 1 workflow.1 >}})\ [@doi:10.1016/j.cels.2025.101294].
This alignment step produces a condition by eigen-state by gene tensor that RISE factorizes into components representing patterns of variation across the three modes.
To overcome the limitations of aggregating data into pre-defined cell types, CCC-RISE infers communication directly from RISE's unsupervised eigen-states rather than individual cells or broad populations ({{< fig 1 workflow.2 >}}).
For every experimental condition and ligand--receptor (LR) pair defined using CellChat's interaction database\ [@doi:10.1038/s41467-021-21246-9], a score is calculated for all combinations of sender and receiver eigen-states by taking the product of the sender's ligand expression with the receiver's receptor expression.
This process yields a four-dimensional tensor of data across experimental conditions, sender eigen-states, receiver eigen-states, and LR pairs.
Finally, to extract patterns from this high-dimensional structure, CCC-RISE employs CPD, which decomposes the tensor into distinct components, each representing a communication program defined by a source of variation across the four modes ({{< fig 1 workflow.3 >}}).

CCC-RISE preserves cell identity through the projection matrices and eigen-state--component associations, which allows for interpretation of CPD factors with single-cell resolution.
The eigen-states define shared gene-expression programs, so the projection matrices weight cells from every condition in a common embedding where proximity reflects transcriptional similarity ({{< fig 1 embedding >}}).
Further, by multiplying the RISE projections with the sender and receiver eigen-state factors, the associations of individual cells with each communication component are recovered ({{< fig 1 cell-mapping >}}).
CCC-RISE's embeddings and factor matrices thus trace LR signaling programs across conditions without losing the granularity of the underlying single-cell data ({{< fig 1 component-interpretation >}}).

### CCC-RISE isolates subpopulation-specific repair signaling in lung transplants

::: {#fig-2}
![](figures/figure2/figure2.svg){width="6.5in"}

**CCC-RISE isolates stable, robust communication programs among epithelial subpopulations.** ({{< panel 2 rise-rank-selection >}}) RISE R^2^X across ranks of the fit on all data and, in BiCV, of the fit on the training block (BiCV train) and its prediction of the held-out block (BiCV test); mean ± SD over 10 repeats per rank.
({{< panel 2 cp-rank-selection.1 >}}) CPD fit R^2^X and aggregate imputation R^2^X of held-out entries over 10 folds across ranks; mean ± SD over 10 repeated fold splits per rank.
({{< panel 2 cp-rank-selection.2 >}}) Largest absolute cosine between the LR pair factors of any two CPD components across ranks, for each of 10 seeded SVD starts per rank (points), colored by whether the start reaches the solution most starts reach at its rank (blue) or another solution (grey); boxes show the median and interquartile range and whiskers show the most extreme values within 1.5-times the interquartile range.
({{< panel 2 cp-minima >}}) Number of the 10 starts reaching each distinct solution across ranks (starts joined at FMS ≥ 0.95): the solution most starts reach (blue, bottom) and each other solution (grey), colored as in ({{< panel 2 cp-rank-selection.2 >}}).
({{< panel 2 cp-factor-matrices >}}) CPD factor matrices representing component loadings of conditions, sender/receiver eigen-states, and LR pairs; conditions are grouped by ALAD status, then six-month outcome (color strips).
({{< panel 2 permutation-lr-significance.1 >}}) Fraction of each LR pair's (n = 513) condition by sender by receiver entries exceeding a null of within-sample cell permutations at p < 0.05 (one-sided empirical test).
({{< panel 2 permutation-lr-significance.2 >}}) Mean observed against mean permuted communication score per LR pair, colored by fraction of entries significant (as above).
({{< panel 2 nichenet >}}) NicheNet target score of each ligand (n = 185) per CPD component on DE between the component's top receiver cells (above the 90th percentile of receiver weight within its receiver cell types) and bottom receiver cells (below the 10th percentile across all cells) (light boxes; points colored and sized by the ligand's weight in the component, opaque for the ligands of its top LR pairs), and on 1,000 rankings with the top/bottom labels shuffled among those cells (grey boxes, pooled).
Boxes show the median and interquartile range and whiskers show the most extreme values within 1.5-times the interquartile range.
\*: q < 0.05 for the ligand-weighted mean score against its 1,000 cell-shuffled values; one-sided empirical test, Benjamini--Hochberg corrected across the five components.
({{< panel 2 sender-receiver-strata >}}) Per-cell component 5 sender against receiver weight.
({{< panel 2 epithelial-markers >}}) Expression of canonical epithelial subtype markers and top LR pair genes in each group.
({{< panel 2 celltype-composition >}}) Annotated cell-type composition of each group, using coarse labels defined by Calabrese et al.\ [@doi:10.1016/j.healun.2024.02.007].
:::

We first applied CCC-RISE to a lung transplant dataset in which conditions represented individual bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) samples from lung-transplant patients with and without acute lung allograft dysfunction (ALAD) ({{< fig alad-cohort cohort >}})\ [@doi:10.1016/j.healun.2024.02.007].
ALAD is an acute decline in lung function following transplantation that either resolves or progresses to chronic lung allograft dysfunction (CLAD), a predominantly irreversible loss of graft function that leads to re-transplantation or death\ [@doi:10.1016/j.trre.2021.100626; @doi:10.1016/j.healun.2022.05.005].
Each sample was defined by its donor's status at the time of collection (control/no ALAD, ALAD-recovered, and ALAD-declined/CLAD) and by its donor's status six months after collection (stable/no ALAD/no CLAD, ALAD-recovered, declined to CLAD, or died) ({{< tbl alad-outcome-groups >}}).
Samples from the lung transplant cohort were composed of broad immune and epithelial cell types whose proportional abundances showed no significant difference between control, declined, and recovered samples ({{< fig alad-cohort celltype-proportions >}}).
We used this cohort to establish how a CCC-RISE model is selected, validated, and interpreted.

We first selected the RISE rank by bi-cross-validation (BiCV), which fits RISE to a random half of all cells and genes and scores the fit's ability to predict the held-out block of cells and genes\ [@doi:10.1214/08-AOAS227].
Held-out R^2^X rose steeply, plateaued around rank 10, and reached its maximum at rank 17, which we used to construct the communication tensor ({{< fig 2 rise-rank-selection >}}, {{< fig rise-factor-matrices >}}).
Seeking a similarly definitive rank-selection criterion for CPD, we evaluated the reconstruction and imputation accuracy (i.e., the accuracy at which the outer product of CPD factors approximates either the original communication tensor or entries held out during fitting, respectively) of CPD models at varying ranks.
Both CPD fit R^2^X and imputation R^2^X generally increased with rank, indicating that higher-rank CPD models did not lose predictive accuracy ({{< fig 2 cp-rank-selection.1 >}}).
However, neither reconstruction metric provided a clear choice for CPD rank, so we instead evaluated collinearity, degeneracy, and instability using the cosine similarity between components across ranks and refactorizations with varying SVD initialization seeds.
The cosine similarity between components in the condition, sender eigen-state, and receiver eigen-state modes increased rapidly with rank, a trend that was stable across starts ({{< fig cmp-stability cp-collinearity >}}).
Conversely, the LR pair mode became collinear in at least one start at rank 6 ({{< fig 2 cp-rank-selection.2 >}}).
As the largest of the four modes, collinearity in LR pairs indicated problematic degeneracy---shared patterns in smaller modes were expected because of the limited number of variation sources amongst conditions and eigen-states, whereas in a collinear regime of the largest mode, it became non-trivial to separate shared communication patterns from artifacts of overfitting.
Further, re-initialized factorizations became unstable at rank 6 and beyond, which, combined with the emergence of collinearity at rank 6, encouraged us to decompose the communication tensor using CPD rank 5 ({{< fig 2 cp-minima >}}, {{< fig 2 cp-factor-matrices >}}).

We next asked whether the communication programs captured by CCC-RISE were stable, robust against cell permutation, and aligned with external biological validation.
At the selected rank, RISE and CPD components were stable over re-initialization and leave-one-patient-out jackknife ({{< fig cmp-stability rise-fms cpd-fms >}}).
To assess robustness, we extended the significance testing of CellPhoneDB and CellChat to continuous eigen-states by shuffling which cell's expression is paired with each eigen-state projection and recomputing the communication tensor\ [@doi:10.1038/s41467-021-21246-9; @doi:10.1038/s41596-020-0292-x].
While only 10% of each LR pair's entries exceeded this null at p < 0.05, mean observed scores exceeded mean null scores for nearly every LR pair, indicating that aggregate LR scores and select individual communication tensor entries were robust to cell permutation ({{< fig 2 permutation-lr-significance >}}).
Finally, we tested whether each component's receiver cells showed transcriptional evidence of ligand signaling by scoring how well differential expression (DE) in the component's top receiver cells recovered each ligand's NicheNet-predicted downstream gene targets ({{< fig 2 nichenet >}})\ [@doi:10.1038/s41592-019-0667-5; @doi:10.1038/s41596-024-01121-9].
Averaged with each ligand's weight in the component, target scores exceeded those obtained with the top and bottom receiver labels shuffled among cells for components 4 and 5 (q = 0.02), with components 1 and 2 trending (q = 0.09 and 0.053) ({{< fig 2 nichenet >}}).
Thus, the receiver cells of components 4 and 5 upregulated the downstream gene targets of the ligands most heavily weighted by those components.
Collectively, these results show that CCC-RISE components are stable, robust to cell permutations, and align with external ligand--gene-target inference data.

RISE eigen-states allow cellular identity to be traced from CPD component weights back to single-cell gene expression without depending on prior annotations.
We illustrate this with component 5, whose sender and receiver loadings were spread across multiple eigen-states, suggesting signaling between populations ({{< fig 2 cp-factor-matrices.2 cp-factor-matrices.3 >}}, {{< fig cmp5-identity eigenstate-scatter cmp-eigenstate-loadings >}}).
Combining these loadings with each cell's RISE projections gave per-cell sender and receiver weights, which few cells carried simultaneously; thresholding defined 67 sender and 58 receiver cells with weights greater than 0.3 times the top cell's sender or receiver weight, respectively ({{< fig 2 sender-receiver-strata >}}).
We found that these groups both expressed canonical epithelial marker genes (FXYD3, EPCAM, and ELF3) at higher levels than all other cells (q < 0.05) ({{< fig cmp5-identity celltype-markers group-vs-rest >}}).
Individually, the groups expressed unique epithelial subpopulation markers indicating communication between ciliated sender cells and basal/secretory receiver cells ({{< fig 2 epithelial-markers >}}, {{< fig cmp5-identity sender-vs-receiver >}}).
These eigen-state--derived epithelial labels aligned closely with available annotations, but represented subpopulations more granular than those defined in the data ({{< fig 2 celltype-composition >}}).
In sum, label-free interpretation of CCC-RISE factors isolated a well-validated CCC program, wherein ciliated epithelial cells secrete betacellulin (BTC) that binds basal and secretory epithelial cells through epidermal growth factor receptors EGFR and ErbB2, inducing tissue repair or fibrosis depending on disease context ({{< fig 2 cp-factor-matrices.4 >}})\ [@doi:10.1165/ajrcmb.20.5.3308; @doi:10.1038/ki.2012.43; @doi:10.3390/cells11060986].

### CCC-RISE identifies a coordinated immune signaling program associated with CLAD

::: {#fig-3}
![](figures/figure3/figure3.svg){width="6.5in"}

**CCC-RISE identifies a coordinated immune signaling axis associated with ALAD outcome.** ({{< panel 3 outcome-association >}}) CPD component 4 condition loadings stratified by six-month outcome: stable (n = 21), ALAD-recovered (n = 12), CLAD (n = 12), and died (n = 2).
Lines connect samples from the same patient, boxes show the median and interquartile range, and whiskers show the most extreme values within 1.5-times the interquartile range.
Associations were tested by one-way ANOVA with Benjamini--Hochberg correction across all outcomes and components.
({{< panel 3 celltype-pacmap.1 >}}) PaCMAP embedding of all cells colored by annotated cell type, drawn in random order so that overlapping cell types remain visible; the dashed box marks the lymphocyte cluster.
({{< panel 3 celltype-pacmap.2 >}}) The lymphocyte cluster colored by each cell's projection onto eigen-state 16, the eigen-state that dominates component 4's sender and receiver factors.
({{< panel 3 lr-loadings >}}) CPD component 4 LR pair loadings against their rank, with the top 10 LR pairs labeled.
({{< panel 3 coordinated-changes.1 >}}) ANOVA association strength of each LR pair's (n = 513) communication score with six-month outcome.
Component 4's top 10 LR pairs and its condition loading association strength are marked.
({{< panel 3 coordinated-changes.2 >}}) Spearman correlation across conditions between each pair of component 4's top 10 LR pairs and between pairs drawn 2,000 times from the remaining LR pairs: at random, matched in expression (each from the 20 pairs nearest a top pair in log mean score), or among the other LR pairs associated with six-month outcome.
Boxes show the median and interquartile range and whiskers show the most extreme values within 1.5-times the interquartile range.
({{< panel 3 lr-permutation >}}) Diamonds: Difference in mean communication score between CLAD/died and stable/recovered samples (n = 14 and 33 samples) of each of component 4's top 10 LR pairs.
Violins: Null differences across 10,000 permutations of outcome labels between patients.
All results are normalized by standard deviations of the null.
q: one-sided empirical test, Benjamini--Hochberg corrected across the 10 pairs.
({{< panel 3 lr-volcano >}}) Ratio of mean communication score in CLAD/died to stable/recovered samples against one-sided empirical p for each CPD component's top 20 LR pairs by loading; component 4's top 10 pairs are labeled where p < 0.05.
:::

Having demonstrated CCC-RISE's capacity to resolve cellular subpopulation heterogeneity, we next asked whether CCC-RISE components were associated with clinical outcome.
ANOVA of each component's condition loadings against patient outcomes revealed significant associations between CPD component 4 and three outcomes after multiple-test correction: six-month outcome, comprising stable, ALAD-recovered, CLAD, and died groups, and six-month and one-year death ({{< fig 3 outcome-association >}}, {{< fig alad-associations cp-associations >}}).
The same test applied to the condition loadings of RISE components yielded no significant associations, suggesting that outcome associations emerged only through inferred intercellular communication ({{< fig alad-associations rise-associations >}}).
Component 4's sender and receiver factors both loaded almost exclusively on eigen-state 16, which projected most strongly onto the lymphocyte cluster of CD4+ T cells, CD8+ T cells, and natural killer (NK) cells ({{< fig 2 cp-factor-matrices.2 cp-factor-matrices.3 >}}, {{< fig 3 celltype-pacmap >}}).
Per-cell sender and receiver weights on component 4 were nearly identical, indicating that the same cells were acting as both senders and receivers of component 4 signals ({{< fig alad-associations sender-receiver-scatter >}}).
Component 4's top LR pairs consisted of markers of immune cell activation/exhaustion (GZMA--F2R, ENTPD1--ADORA2A, and NECTIN3--TIGIT), immune-activating chemokines and receptors (CCL4/CCL5--CCR4/CCR5 and CXCL13--CXCR3), and activating co-stimulatory ligands and receptors (CD70--CD27 and TNFSF4--TNFRSF4) ({{< fig 3 lr-loadings >}}).
CPD component 4 thus collectively represents an inflammatory communication axis within activated immune populations that is upregulated in CLAD-positive and deceased lung-transplant recipients.
Further, this communication program aligns with a previously identified increase in CD8+ T cell activation and NK cell cytotoxicity during the ALAD--CLAD transition\ [@doi:10.1016/j.healun.2024.02.007].

CPD groups LR pairs based on covariation across conditions, senders, and receivers rather than by their association with outcome.
Indeed, while some of component 4's top LR pairs exhibited strong individual association with outcome, they were not the only highly associated LR pairs and were not defined as a group by their ability to stratify patients ({{< fig 3 coordinated-changes.1 >}}).
Individual outcome association therefore did not explain which LR pairs component 4 grouped together.
Instead, component 4's top LR pairs were more strongly correlated with one another across conditions than randomly drawn LR pairs, LR pairs matched in mean communication score (LR expression), or other LR pairs with a significant outcome association ({{< fig 3 coordinated-changes.2 >}}).
The expression-matched baseline excludes shared abundance as the source of this coordination, and the outcome-associated baseline shows that it is not explained by a common association with outcome.
These results indicate that, by modeling variation across conditions, cells, and LR pairs, CCC-RISE isolates coordinated communication axes from sets of individually varying programs.

Given the limited size of the ALAD cohort and the small number of patients in the "died" group, we tested whether the component 4 association could be explained by patient covariates, individual patients, or random patient grouping.
No patient covariate (besides Caucasian ethnicity, which was weakly associated with one-year death) was associated with outcome, even before multiple-test correction ({{< fig alad-associations covariates >}}).
Further, the six-month outcome association remained significant in 42 of 45 leave-one-patient-out jackknife replicates ({{< fig anova-stability effect-size-distributions significant-fraction >}}).
Of the three exceptions, one patient fell in the died group and carried the largest component 4 condition loading.
While these associations did hinge on one especially highly weighted patient, the coordinated program represented by the associated component is a real biological pattern present in the expression data.
We next applied scDiffCom's condition-label--permutation scheme to our communication tensor to test whether each LR pair's difference in communication score between CLAD/died and stable/recovered samples exceeded those obtained with permuted patient outcome labels\ [@doi:10.1038/s43587-023-00514-x].
Eight of component 4's ten top LR pairs had higher communication scores in CLAD/died samples than in stable/recovered samples (q < 0.05), indicating that communication scores constructed through RISE exceeded chance in their ability to stratify patients ({{< fig 3 lr-permutation lr-volcano >}}).

Choice of CCC scoring method used to construct the communication tensor is a known source of disagreement between tools, so we asked whether the program described by component 4 was dependent on our choice of expression-product scoring\ [@doi:10.1038/s41467-022-30755-0; @doi:10.1038/s41576-020-00292-x].
We compared four approaches used to convert expression to LR interaction scores: product, used by CCC-RISE and NATMI\ [@doi:10.1038/s41467-020-18873-z]; mean, used by Tensor-cell2cell and CellPhoneDB\ [@doi:10.1038/s41467-022-31369-2; @doi:10.1038/s41596-020-0292-x]; geometric mean (gmean), used by scDiffCom\ [@doi:10.1038/s43587-023-00514-x]; and the Hill function-inspired score used by CellChat\ [@doi:10.1038/s41467-021-21246-9].
Upon recomputing the communication tensor from a single RISE fit using each scoring method, we observed that each alternate score generally yielded a CPD fit closely matching that of CCC-RISE's product ({{< fig ccc-scoring factor-match >}}).
Further, the recovered component remained associated with six-month outcome under every score, although the mean and gmean scores also associated component 3 with outcome ({{< fig ccc-scoring anova >}}).
The alternate scores captured LR pairs similar to those of the product score, especially in components 4 and 5 ({{< fig ccc-scoring interpretation.1 >}}).
For component 4, every score identified T and NK cells as senders, and the Hill score identified the same cells as receivers, whereas the mean and gmean scores instead implicated epithelial receivers ({{< fig ccc-scoring interpretation.2 >}}).
Overall, CCC-RISE's expression product agreed closely with CellChat's expression Hill function, and even lower-FMS scores closely matched the LR pairs and either the sender or receiver eigen-states of components 4 and 5.

### CCC-RISE uncovers hormonal communication that varies continuously over cells in IBD

::: {#fig-4}
![](figures/figure4/figure4.svg){width="6.5in"}

**Complementary CCC-RISE components describe states along a continuous population of hormone-secreting enteroendocrine cells in IBD.** ({{< panel 4 cp-factor-matrices >}}) CPD factor matrices representing component loadings of conditions, sender/receiver eigen-states, and LR pairs.
({{< panel 4 ee-state-map >}}) RISE projection embeddings of EE, EC, and tuft cells colored by ({{< panel 4 ee-state-map.1 >}}) cell type as annotated in the IBDverse data, ({{< panel 4 ee-state-map.2 >}}) component 3 sender weight, or ({{< panel 4 ee-state-map.3 >}}) component 4 sender weight.
({{< panel 4 hormone-expression-map >}}) RISE projection embeddings of EE and EC cells colored by PYY (left) or GCG (right) expression normalized to the expression in the top 1% of expressing cells.
({{< panel 4 hormone-angle-scatter >}}) Each EE cell's component 3/4 sender weight normalized to the maximum weight, colored by polar angle where the polar magnitude is at least 0.3 (dotted arc).
Shaded region excludes cells exceeding 180°.
Dotted ray and arc indicate an example polar coordinate: (0.3, 45°).
({{< panel 4 hormone-angle-hist >}}) Distribution of EE cells with polar magnitude of at least 0.3 over polar angles, colored by angle-based thresholds at 30 and 60°.
({{< panel 4 hormone-extreme-markers >}}) Expression of crypt, intermediate (int.), and villus EE markers and BMP target genes in each group.
Markers were curated from Beumer et al.\ (2018, 2020), Gehart et al., and Krzak et al.\ [@doi:10.1038/s41556-018-0143-y; @doi:10.1016/j.cell.2020.04.036; @doi:10.1016/j.cell.2018.12.029; @doi:10.1038/s41588-026-02634-7].
Genes shown differ between villus-like and crypt-like cells at q < 0.05 (Mann--Whitney U test, Benjamini--Hochberg corrected across all markers tested).
({{< panel 4 niches-concordance >}}) NICHES concordance of the component 3 and 4 sender (S) and receiver (R) populations (diamonds), as predicted by their fine cell-type labels (circles) and lineages (ticks), and under 1,000 random RISE directions matched for cell type (grey bars, 5th--95th percentiles).
Filled diamonds: q < 0.05; one-sided empirical test against the random directions, Benjamini--Hochberg corrected across the 12 populations of the six components.
({{< panel 4 niches-orderings >}}) NICHES concordance of each population's number of top-ranked cells under five orderings: a random RISE direction (median of 200, not matched for cell type), the CCC-RISE weight, the positive part of either multiplied by the cell's ligand or receptor expression, and that expression alone; left, each population's NICHES-positive cells and the share of all cells in the cohort that are NICHES-positive.
:::

We next sought to extend CCC-RISE to an inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) dataset (IBDverse), representing a biologically distinct disease context with enhanced statistical power compared with the ALAD dataset\ [@doi:10.1038/s41588-026-02634-7].
In the IBD data, conditions comprised terminal-ileum punch biopsies from individual donors of three groups: healthy (no Crohn's Disease; CD), CD uninflamed, and CD inflamed ({{< fig ibd-rank-selection cohort >}}).
We selected the IBD ranks with the same BiCV and CPD analyses as for ALAD to construct a CCC-RISE model on IBDverse while avoiding overfitting.
Unlike for ALAD, held-out R^2^X in the RISE BiCV sweep plateaued without a clear maximum, so we used rank 60, the smallest rank within one standard error of the largest held-out R^2^X (rank 85), to decompose the normalized expression tensor ({{< fig ibd-rank-selection rise-rank-selection bicv-test >}}).
The CPD LR pair mode first became collinear at rank 7, where no more than 3 of the 10 starts also reached any one solution, so we decomposed the communication tensor at rank 6 ({{< fig ibd-rank-selection cp-collinearity mode-collinearity >}}).
CCC-RISE yielded components that described healthy and inflamed gut communication programs, including opposing activating/inhibitory immune signaling (components 1 and 5), myeloid--driven axon maintenance (component 2), and hormone secretion (components 3--4) ({{< fig 4 cp-factor-matrices >}}, {{< fig ibd-rank-selection factors eigenstate-heatmap >}}).

The data describe a number of diverse communication programs, so we tested the associations of CPD condition with biopsy type to narrow our interpretation onto clinically relevant programs.
While many components tracked three-way inflammation status and distinguished healthy from CD samples, only components 3 and 4 were able to differentiate uninflamed from inflamed CD samples ({{< fig ibd-associations cp-associations >}}).
While ALAD condition weights generally showed a positive correlation with disease severity, IBD condition weights of components 3 and 4 were higher in uninflamed than inflamed CD samples, indicating a loss of communication following inflammation ({{< fig ibd-associations status-loadings >}}).
Unlike in the ALAD data, cell-type compositions directly tracked condition state: immune cells increased and epithelial cells decreased in abundance with inflammation ({{< fig ibd-associations lineage-proportions covariates >}}).
Thus, CPD components were associated with inflammation status and tracked cell-type composition, as expected for a disease characterized by immune-cell invasion and epithelial cell death\ [@doi:10.1016/j.immuni.2023.01.002].

CPD components 3 and 4 represented distinct, but complementary, hormone-signaling axes.
They were loaded onto similar sender eigen-states---albeit with distinct distributions---that collectively defined a subpopulation of enteroendocrine (EE) cells ({{< fig ibd-hormone-axes eigenstate-loadings eigenstate-composition >}}).
Conversely their receiver eigen-states were entirely distinct and uniquely loaded either enterochromaffin (EC) cells (component 3) or tuft cells (component 4) ({{< fig ibd-hormone-axes eigenstate-loadings eigenstate-composition >}}).
We therefore restricted our analysis to EE, EC, and tuft cells (as annotated in the IBDverse data) and visualized single-cell heterogeneity in the component 3/4 signaling axis using RISE projection embeddings ({{< fig 4 ee-state-map.1 >}}, {{< fig ibd-hormone-axes cell-map >}}, {{< panel ibd-hormone-axes type-map >}}).
Cells with high sender weights in either components 3 or 4 inhabited distinct regions of the broader EE cell cluster, but partially overlapped with each other, indicating that the components represented a non-exclusive pair of EE subpopulations ({{< fig 4 ee-state-map.2 ee-state-map.3 >}}).
Further, cells with the highest expression of PYY predominantly overlapped with those of high component 3 sender weight, and those with high GCG (GLP-1) expression overlapped with those of high component 4 sender weight, indicating that sender groups were primarily defined by the gene expression of those two hormones ({{< fig 4 hormone-expression-map >}}).
Component 3 and 4 receiver cells were trivially exclusive, and also matched the expression levels of their respective receptors (NPY1R and GLP1R) ({{< fig ibd-hormone-axes receiver-maps.1 receptor-maps.1 >}}, {{< panel ibd-hormone-axes receiver-maps.2 receptor-maps.2 >}}).

We went on to characterize the overlapping EE subpopulations represented by components 3 and 4.
There was no clear separation of cells by component 3/4 per-cell sender weight, indicating that the components were consistent with the hormonal plasticity of EE cells within the GLP-1-producing lineage ({{< fig 4 hormone-angle-scatter >}})\ [@doi:10.1210/endrev/bnaa018; @doi:10.1016/j.cell.2018.12.029].
Transforming the sender weight axes to polar coordinates and measuring the distribution of cells over polar angles revealed that two states dominated the continuum of cell identities ({{< fig 4 hormone-angle-hist >}}, {{< fig ibd-hormone-axes magnitude-hist >}}).
While we recognize the continuous nature of these populations, we attempted to binarize the cells into component 3-high, component 4-high, both, or neither groups using their polar coordinates in order to annotate the cells against canonical markers ({{< fig 4 hormone-angle-hist >}}).
The four groups of cells were characterized by distinct gene expression: component 3-high cells expressed hormones associated with villus EE cells, component 4-high cells expressed crypt-associated genes, and mixed cells expressed CCK, which marks the intermediate stage between GLP-1-producing and villus cells ({{< fig 4 hormone-extreme-markers >}})\ [@doi:10.1038/s41556-018-0143-y; @doi:10.1016/j.cell.2020.04.036; @doi:10.1016/j.cell.2018.12.029; @doi:10.1038/s41588-026-02634-7].
Further, the crypt-to-villus transition is driven by BMP activity, and we saw a stepwise increase in expression of BMP targets from crypt-like to mixed to villus-like cells ({{< fig 4 hormone-extreme-markers >}})\ [@doi:10.1038/s41556-018-0143-y; @doi:10.1016/j.cell.2020.04.036].
All genes except the intermediate marker CCK remained differentially expressed (q < 0.05) between crypt- and villus-like cells across magnitude thresholds up to 0.9, after which low cell counts reduce statistical power ({{< fig ibd-hormone-axes marker-floor-sweep >}}).
In agreement with the loss of function following inflammation indicated by component 3 associations ({{< fig ibd-associations status-loadings.1 >}}), component 3-high cells gradually contributed less to the overall EE population in a step-wise manner over healthy, CD uninflamed, and CD inflamed biopsies, indicating that more-exposed, villus-like cells are more sensitive to inflammatory pressure compared with other EE subpopulations ({{< fig ibd-hormone-axes extreme-share >}}).

Although CCC-RISE assigns cells by their overall transcriptional state rather than their own ligand or receptor expression, we inferred that the cells it weighted most heavily as senders and receivers express the components' ligands and receptors themselves ({{< fig 4 hormone-expression-map >}}, {{< fig ibd-hormone-axes receptor-maps.1 >}}, {{< panel ibd-hormone-axes receptor-maps.2 >}}).
As a partial, independent check of this, we thresholded each component's per-cell sender and receiver weights into populations at 0.3 of each weight's largest value ({{< fig niches-ibd weight-scatters >}}) and compared them with NICHES.
NICHES is blind to state and instead scores each cell as a sender and as a receiver from its own expression of a set of LR pairs\ [@doi:10.1093/bioinformatics/btac775].
We ran it on each component's carrying pairs, the fewest LR pairs that together carry 90% of the component's squared LR pair loading, and measured each population's NICHES concordance as the share of its cells that NICHES scored above zero.
The component 3 and 4 populations held more NICHES-positive cells than their fine cell-type labels predict (component 3 senders 0.80 against 0.52 and component 4 senders 0.73 against 0.46; component 3 receivers 0.57 against 0.38 and component 4 receivers 0.25 against 0.16), and more than when random directions in RISE space replaced the component's loadings, matched for cell type (q ≤ 0.026) ({{< fig 4 niches-concordance >}}).
Within the same cell types, the component's own direction therefore picked out cells with NICHES signal more often than arbitrary directions did.
Across all six components, populations exceeded their labels' prediction (eight of twelve with q < 0.05) ({{< fig 4 niches-concordance >}}, {{< fig niches-ibd concordance >}}), and this measured gap held at every population threshold from 0.1 to 0.6 ({{< fig niches-ibd tau-sweep >}}).
Weighting even a random RISE direction by a cell's ligand or receptor expression brought 9 of the 12 populations close to the concordance of that expression alone ({{< fig 4 niches-orderings >}}, {{< fig niches-ibd orderings >}}), so for these populations concordance follows from reading expression.
CCC-RISE weights, however, reached higher concordance than random directions for every population without reading each cell's expression (0.02--0.80 against 0.00--0.07).
In sum, CCC-RISE components 3 and 4 described sender cells on a continuum between two prevailing states---crypt-like producers of GCG communicating with tuft cells and villus-like producers of PYY communicating with EC cells---and their populations held more NICHES-positive cells than their fine cell-type labels predict.

### CCC-RISE resolves communication programs that label-based methods reach only in part

::: {#fig-5}
![](figures/figure5/figure5.svg){width="6.5in"}

LR columns are named by method (P, T, S) and number.
({{< panel 5 program-map >}}) Each CCC-RISE component's largest cos^2^ (squared cosine of LR pair loadings) with one LR column of any fine-label fit, against its label ceiling, the per-cell weight R^2^: the share of variance in its per-cell sender (circles) and receiver (squares) weights held by means over sample and fine label; a line joins a component's two points.
({{< panel 5 column-census >}}) Every comparator LR column, classed by the first rule it meets; numbers give the columns in each class.
({{< panel 5 best-column >}}) Each CCC-RISE component's largest cos^2^ with one LR column of each fit.
({{< panel 5 pair-columns >}}) Carrying pairs of ALAD components 3 and 4 in the component and in the STACCato columns carrying them, each column scaled to its heaviest pair.
Red outlines and bold names mark the columns tested in ({{< panel 5 program-covariation >}}).
({{< panel 5 program-covariation >}}) Mean pairwise Spearman correlation across samples ($\bar{\rho}$) of the carrying pairs of each component or column, over all pairs of LR pairs (top) and over those sharing no gene (bottom).
Ticks show the stricter null, the larger 95th percentile of 2,000 random and 2,000 expression-matched draws; filled points are above it.
({{< panel 5 flow-alad >}}) BTC--EGFR in STACCato's S10 (fine) and in ALAD component 5 among the 288 cells labeled lung epithelium.

Bars show fractions of each cell type's cells: the 3,058 EE cells in villus-like (510), mixed (346), crypt-like (413), and other (1,789) groups, as in {{< fig 4 hormone-angle-hist >}}, and the 546 of 972 EC and 1,268 of 4,712 tuft cells past the receiver cutoff.

Labeled: the populations of the components in ({{< panel 5 flow-alad >}}) and ({{< panel 5 flow-ibd >}}); S, sender; R, receiver.

Having found programs in both cohorts that span or subdivide annotated cell types, we next asked what of them would be lost by pooling cells by annotation, as existing tensor methods do.
We compared CCC-RISE with three tensor methods that pool cells by sample and annotated cell type, each fit to both cohorts at coarse (8 ALAD and 7 IBD cell types) and fine (26 and 54) labels.
Pseudobulk CPD scored mean expression per sample and cell type and was fit and ranked exactly as CCC-RISE's CPD, so it differs from CCC-RISE only in the tensor it decomposes and serves as an ablation of cell state.
Tensor-cell2cell and STACCato, the closest published tensor methods, each used its own score, decomposition, and rank selection, with the departures from their published analyses described in Methods ({{< fig comparator-rank-selection pb-fit-coarse stac-shares-fine >}})\ [@doi:10.1038/s41467-022-31369-2; @doi:10.1016/j.ajhg.2026.05.005].
Because STACCato's Tucker model does not tie its factors into components, we compared methods through their LR columns, named by method (P, T, or S) and number, and we name CCC-RISE components by cohort.
To locate where pooling could fall short, we placed each CCC-RISE component on two measures: the largest squared cosine (cos^2^) between its LR pair loadings and those of any fine-label LR column, and its label ceiling, the per-cell weight R^2^ held by means over sample and fine label, which bounds what any method pooling cells by sample and annotation can represent ({{< fig 5 program-map >}}).
Only ALAD and IBD component 2 were within reach on both measures.
ALAD components 3 and 4 had cells that labels describe (R^2^ 0.68--0.85) but LR pairs that no fine-label column held (cos^2^ 0.41 and 0.43), whereas ALAD component 5 and the senders of IBD components 3 and 4 had LR pairs that one column held (cos^2^ 0.90--1.00) but cells that labels did not (R^2^ 0.24--0.39).
Coarse labels held less (label ceiling at most 0.09 for IBD components; {{< fig comparator-map coarse-map >}}), and no comparator column reproduced more than 0.21 of any component's per-cell weights ({{< fig comparator-map sender-ceiling receiver-ceiling >}}).
Most CCC-RISE components were therefore out of reach of labels, either because of how their LR pairs were arranged or because their cells lay below the annotation.

We next asked whether any comparator, read on its own, recovers CCC-RISE's components.
We classed every comparator LR column by its containment in CCC-RISE's LR pair span, its overlap with one component's carrying pairs, its breadth, and its share of homophilic pairs ({{< fig 5 column-census >}}, {{< fig comparator-classes span-containment homophilic-share >}}), and found each component's best column in every fit ({{< fig 5 best-column >}}).
Of 87 comparator LR columns, 33 were the same as or part of a CCC-RISE program, and the other 54 were homophilic adhesion (16), broad (20), single-pair (5), or mixed-pair (13) columns, which often differed between a method's coarse and fine fits ({{< fig comparator-map alad-columns >}}, {{< panel comparator-map ibd-columns >}}).
Of the 20 pseudobulk CPD columns, 18 rested on one or two LR pairs, and the method held ALAD components 1 and 2 and IBD components 2 and 6 (cos^2^ 0.78--1.00), but none of ALAD components 4 and 5 or IBD components 3 and 4 (cos^2^ 0.00).
Tensor-cell2cell columns were all broad and tracked each sample's detection depth more than those of any other method (median absolute ρ 0.37--0.74, against 0.05--0.26 for CCC-RISE and the other comparators; {{< fig comparator-split depth-tracking >}}).
STACCato held the components built on one LR axis (cos^2^ 0.88--1.00), including, at fine labels, the hormone pairs of IBD components 3 and 4, but no method held ALAD component 4 (cos^2^ ≤ 0.43) or IBD components 1 and 5 (≤ 0.51).
Each comparator thus recovered a different subset of CCC-RISE's components, and only components built on one LR axis.

We then asked whether the components of mixed LR pairs that no single column held are coordinated programs that label-based methods split apart.
We assigned each of a component's carrying pairs to the STACCato column that loads it most ({{< fig 5 pair-columns >}}) and extended the co-variation test of {{< fig 3 coordinated-changes.2 >}} to the carrying pairs of every component and column ({{< fig 5 program-covariation >}}).
ALAD component 4, the lymphocyte program associated with six-month outcome ({{< fig 3 outcome-association >}}), split between S15 (59%) and S12 (32%) at coarse labels, and at fine labels S14 carried 91% of it but put 56% of that loading in CD70--CD27 alone (cos^2^ 0.43 with component 4).
Component 4's six carrying pairs co-varied across samples at a mean ρ of 0.80, 0.27 above the stricter of the random and expression-matched nulls, over all pairs and over pairs sharing no gene.
ALAD component 3, spread over five coarse and six fine columns, was above the covariation null by 0.05, whereas every STACCato column carrying either component's pairs fell below the null (by 0.10--0.44 over all pairs and 0.18--0.48 over pairs sharing no gene).
Nevertheless, co-variation itself was not a unique finding of CCC-RISE as some columns of every method passed on ALAD ({{< fig comparator-covariation pairs-used disjoint >}}), as did P3 on IBD (0.46 above the stricter null; {{< fig comparator-covariation ibd-pairs-used ibd-disjoint >}}).
The mixed IBD components 1 and 5 were merged and divided between STACCato columns and co-varied only weakly ({{< fig comparator-split mixed-pairs mixed-covariation >}}).
CCC-RISE thus kept the pairs of the ALAD outcome-associated program (component 4) together as a coordinated set where label-based columns divided them.
This is a clear result on ALAD that IBD neither supports nor contradicts.

Finally, we assessed whether CCC-RISE resolves sender and receiver populations below the annotation for components whose LR pairs a comparator did hold.
We compared the whole labels each STACCato column assigns with CCC-RISE's populations ({{< fig 5 flow-alad flow-ibd >}}).
STACCato's S10 (fine) held BTC--EGFR (cos^2^ 0.90 with ALAD component 5) but reported it from lung epithelium to itself, whereas component 5 resolved the ciliated-like senders and basal/secretory-like receivers of {{< fig 2 sender-receiver-strata >}} into subpopulations finer than the annotation ({{< fig 2 celltype-composition >}}).
Component 5's ligand targets were raised in its 29 top receiver cells (0.078 above shuffled cells) but not in the label's 288 cells under the STACCato columns carrying its pairs (−0.007 and 0.028; {{< fig comparator-nichenet closest-columns >}}), whereas components 2 and 3, whose cells labels describe, gained nothing over their columns in this regard.
These differences were not formally tested, but in the cell-shuffle test of {{< fig 2 nichenet >}}, applied to every column, only components 4 and 5 and the pseudobulk CPD P4 columns passed ({{< fig comparator-nichenet cell-shuffle prior-shuffle >}}).
Likewise, STACCato's fine fit held PYY--NPY1R and GCG--GLP1R whole (cos^2^ 0.99 and 1.00) but sent both hormones from one EE label, whereas CCC-RISE separated their senders along a villus-to-crypt-like continuum.
The IBD component 3 and 4 populations also agreed with NICHES more than their labels predict ({{< fig 5 niches-fraction >}}).
Overall, 17 of 22 CCC-RISE defined populations across both cohorts held more NICHES-positive cells than their fine labels predict, including every IBD population and ALAD component 5's senders and receivers (0.16 and 0.29, against 0.06 and 0.07) ({{< fig 5 niches-fraction >}}).
Where a comparator held a component's LR pairs, CCC-RISE therefore resolved its cells below the annotation, and these cells typically carried more NICHES signal than their labels predict and more downstream target signal.

Last, it is important to report what the comparators found that CCC-RISE did not.
We examined the 18 single-pair and mixed-pair comparator columns that were neither part of a CCC-RISE program nor adhesion or broad ({{< fig comparator-missed column-contents >}}).
Many of their LR pairs were already in CCC-RISE components, such as CXCL9/10/11--CXCR3 in ALAD component 3, and most of the rest had weak support in literature or rested on single biopsies.
Two axes, however, were most likely missed.
AREG--EGFR was found by coarse STACCato columns on ALAD and is reportedly raised in CLAD\ [@doi:10.1111/ajt.15667].
P3 (coarse), S5 (coarse), and S8 (fine) also represented a neutrophil-recruitment axis on IBD that joins the CXCR1/CXCR2 ligands CXCL5, CXCL3, and CXCL2\ [@doi:10.1038/s41591-021-01520-5], with SAA1--FPR2, through which serum amyloid A attracts neutrophils and monocytes\ [@doi:10.1084/jem.189.2.395].
IBD component 5 covers this axis only in part, through CXCL8 and CXCL1.
Association with clinical groups was not solely unique to CCC-RISE either as some of these missed columns were associated with the same outcomes as ALAD component 4 and IBD components 1, 3, 4, and 5 ({{< fig comparator-missed alad-associations ibd-associations >}}).
Together, one CCC-RISE fit captured coordinated programs of mixed LR pairs and populations below the cell-type annotations that three separate label-based methods reached only in part, while those methods were able to find two axes that CCC-RISE partially missed.
